answer: Before 1948 most Jewish-held land was bought: of 1,731,300 dunams at the end of 1944, the Survey of Palestine counts 1,556,700 as purchased and 174,600 as government concessions. That is 6.6 percent of Palestine's area; other counts run from about 1.49 to 2 million dunams, by date and definition. The share is of the whole country, nearly half of it desert (the Survey puts the Beersheba desert at about 12,077 of 26,320 square kilometres), and some land was state land, not Arab-owned. Most purchases were from large landowners, many of them absentee, and the Jewish National Fund held its land as inalienable Jewish property. But sales displaced Arab tenant farmers: in 1930 Hope Simpson concluded that of 688 tenant families on Jezreel-valley land Jews had bought, 309 had joined the landless, and area officers counted 1,270 farmers displaced. In 1940 Britain restricted sales.

facts.text: Counts of Jewish-owned land differ by source, date and definition, so they are not a trend: 1,731,300 dunams at the end of 1944 (the Survey of Palestine), of which 1,556,700 were purchased and 174,600 were government concessions, 6.6 percent of Palestine's area; about 1,588,000 dunams registered in Jewish names at the end of 1945 (also the Survey, which assumes 650,000 dunams were owned before 1920 and excludes land held by Jews as tenants but not registered); 1,514,247 dunams on 1 April 1943 (Survey, vol. II); 1,491,699 dunams on 1 April 1945 (Village Statistics, as quoted by a UN study; it is lower than the Survey's 1943 figure for reasons the sources do not give); and about 2 million dunams by May 1948 (Stein's estimate: his text calls it purchased, his table heads it 'total land accumulated to date from all sources'). The 6.6 percent is a share of the whole land area, including desert and state land; it is not a share of farmland or of privately owned land.

facts.text: Palestine's total land area was about 26,320 square kilometres, of which about 12,077 square kilometres lay in the desert of Beersheba (the Negev); the Survey elsewhere gives 13,743 for the rest, which sums to 25,820, a 500 square kilometre inconsistency in the Survey itself. The Survey adds that there may be private claims to over 2,000 square kilometres of that desert, cultivated from time to time. The UN committee called the Negev south of latitude 31 desert land of little agricultural value, and Stein notes the land Jews bought was not south of Beersheba. So 6.6 percent is a share of a country nearly half of which was desert.

facts.text: The land not owned by Jews was not all Arab-owned. facts.text: Purchases from large owners cost Arab tenant farmers their holdings. In 1930 Hope Simpson, reading the Jewish Agency's own list of 688 Arab tenants of the Jezreel (Esdraelon) valley villages bought by Jewish buyers, concluded that only 379 families still farmed and 309 had joined the landless classes; the government's own area officers counted 1,270 farmers displaced from those villages. The Agency's memorandum had said very few of those traced were landless, and Hope Simpson wrote that the Jewish authorities paid high prices and the duty to protect the tenants lay with the government.

facts.text: Britain created an official register of 'landless Arabs' in 1931 (Lewis French, Director of Development); by 1 January 1936 it had admitted 664 of 3,271 applicants and disallowed 2,607. The register excluded, among others, persons displaced by purchases by non-Jews, persons who were not tenant cultivators at the time of sale (owners who let their land, ploughmen, those already become labourers), and persons who had found other land or permanent employment.

facts.text: The Shaw Commission (1930), sent after the 1929 violence, is reported by three summaries (the Encyclopaedia Judaica, Shira Klein's COJS essay and an Emory Center for Israel Education timeline; the report itself was not read) to have found that the Arabs' sense of insecurity was caused by the Jewish national home, and particularly by Jewish immigration and land settlement. The Encyclopaedia Judaica quotes the report: the Arabs feared that by 'Jewish immigration and land purchases they may be deprived of their livelihood and placed under the economic domination of the Jews'; it also quotes the report's fundamental cause as 'the Arab feeling of animosity and hostility towards the Jews consequent upon the disappointment of their political and national aspirations and fear for their economic future'.

Stein, the only source on this point, says the regulations were rigorously circumvented by legal ruses.

contested.text: How much of the displacement purchases caused is disputed. Hope Simpson (1930) concluded, from the Jewish Agency's own list, that 309 of 688 tenant families on the Esdraelon villages had joined the landless, and reported the area officers' count of 1,270 farmers displaced; the Agency's memorandum, which he quotes, said very few of those traced were landless. Stein says that on the 200,000 dunams of Sursock land fewer than 700 Arab tenants worked, perhaps 5,000 people in all, but the same passage records 900 Arabs living on 14,000 dunams at Shatta and 1,200 Bedouin families at Wadi Hawarith when the JNF bought those lands in 1929-1930. In its official 1937 summary the Peel Commission judged that the shortage of land was due less to purchase by Jews than to the increase in the Arab population, while urging care for tenants. The 1936 register of landless Arabs admitted 664 applicants under a strict definition.

could_not_verify: The shares bought from absentee owners, from resident large owners and from small farmers: I found only Stein's 'more than 60 percent from absentee landlords in the 1920s' and his rejection of the 9.4 percent peasant figure. The Granott breakdown (52.6, 24.6, 13.4 and 9.4 percent) and Porath's work are not on any readable page I found, so they are not quoted.

The Shaw Commission's own words on a 'landless and discontented class' appear only on a page I could not read (a Middle Eastern Studies article); I cite what the Shaw Commission is reported to have found by two readable scholarly summaries instead.
Lewis French's report itself (1931-32) was not found; his work is described through the Survey of Palestine, which counts the registered landless at 664.

Share of land that was state land: the Survey gives public land in settled areas (over 660 square kilometres) and state domain in dunams, not a single percentage of the whole country; the table that has Jewish land separately lumps all non-Jews. I could not find a reliable single figure for state land.
The state-land fact has three reliable sites only if one counts the two volumes of the Survey as one; the Village Statistics reprint is advocacy and not counted.

Figures for Jewish-owned land differ (1.49, 1.51, 1.59, 1.73 and 2.0 million dunams): the card says which source gives which, but I could not tell from the pages whether Stein's 2 million is purchases or holdings, or whether Jewish totals before 1920 (650,000 assumed) are firm.
The Survey of Palestine is cited from the Berman Jewish Policy Archive's scan of a 1946 British government publication; I found no archive.org copy readable here.

Reviewer: no Palestinian or Bedouin scholar on tenant displacement or on Bedouin land claims in the Beersheba area is quoted; Khalidi appears in one line. The card leans on Stein and on British government documents.
Reviewer: Hope Simpson also criticised JNF lease terms (no Arab labour); that is in the cited report but not carried as a fact.
not_claimed: This card does not say the land was 'empty' or that all sellers were willing; Hope Simpson and the Peel report document displacement and its limits.
It does not say purchases were illegal; they were legal under the Mandate, and restricted from 1940.
It does not cover the land that changed hands in and after 1948.
It does not say 6.6 percent is the share of cultivable land; the Survey's own table shows Jewish ownership of cultivable categories was larger.

skeptic.notes: Read 2+ sources for every fact (12) in context, including both volumes of the Survey. Figures check out against the Survey. Five Jewish-owned totals: all five are on their pages; they differ by date and definition (concessions, registered vs held, assumption of 650,000 before 1920, Stein's 'all sources'); the 1,491,699 for April 1945 is lower than the 1,514,247 for April 1943 and the sources do not say why; the fact now says so and says they are not a trend. 6.6 percent is the Survey's share of total land area (1,731,300 of 26,320 km2); the fact now says it is not of farmland or private land. [must-fix] Old answer began 'Jews bought land; they did not seize it' but 174,600 dunams (10 percent of the 1944 total) were government concessions, and the UN study on the card says the rest not bought came by Mandatory cessions or from religious charities; reworded to 'most ... was bought'. [must-fix] Contested[0] said 'both agree tenants were displaced; they differ on blame' with no quote from Khalidi or Stein saying so; removed. Added a blame entry from Hope Simpson (the Jewish authorities 'have nothing with which to reproach themselves'; the duty was the government's), which the card omitted and which the Israeli side would cite. [must-fix] Palestinian side: Stein's 'fewer than 700 tenants, perhaps 5,000 people' (Sursock) was quoted while the same passage records 900 Arabs on 14,000 dunams (Shatta) and 1,200 Bedouin families on 30,000 dunams (Wadi Hawarith); added. Hope Simpson's 309 of 688 is his reading of the Jewish Agency's own list, which said 'very few' were landless; both now shown. [must-fix] Fact 10 (Shaw) rests on three summaries, none of which is the report; now said in the text, with the report's stated primary cause (political and national aspirations) alongside the economic fear. [should-fix] Fact 2 (state land): the two Survey volumes and a PLO-reprint (advocacy) are one origin; 660 km2 and 616,000 dunums are different counts; no whole-country state-land figure exists on the card. Fact 6: the 90 percent debt figure is JNF buyer Hankin's claim to Hope Simpson, not Stein's finding; fixed. Fact 11: 'got around them' rests on Stein alone; said. Fact 1: Survey internal inconsistency (12,077 + 13,743 = 25,820, not 26,320) and the Survey's 2,000 km2 of possible private claims in the Negev are now on the card. Stein's 2 million: 'purchased' in text, 'from all sources' in his table. [should-fix] Missing: JNF lease terms (Hope Simpson), the Peel finding that tenants were displaced, and any Bedouin-side source. Stein supplies five facts and three of the contested entries: one scholar. 'heard' (Khalidi on the Jewish Colonization Agency) is a weak form of the claim; the stronger one, 1948, is deferred to another card. Strongest objections: Palestinian side, tenant displacement and Bedouin claims thinly sourced; Israeli side, concessions and Hope Simpson's 'nothing to reproach' were missing.

citer.notes: 6 answer sentences, each tied to facts. Removed/reworded: 'they did not seize it' (no fact says nothing was seized; concessions are in fact 0); 'roughly 6 to 7 percent' (the Survey says 6.6; the 2 million estimate is 7.6 percent of 26.3 million, outside the range) replaced by the Survey's own 6.6 and 'other counts run from 1.49 to 2 million'; 'sales cost Arab tenant farmers their holdings' now rests on the Esdraelon evidence stated; 'Historians dispute how many were displaced and who was to blame' removed from the answer (only contested carries it); 'state land is part of the rest' reworded (the Negev is largely state or unsettled land too). The cultivable-land fact (3) is not used by the answer; should-fix: say that Jewish share of citrus land was about half and of taxable cereal land about 13 percent, so 6.6 percent is not the share of farmland.
